claims.text: Homogenized HfNbTaTiZr has a high degree of configurational disorder and inherent local lattice distortions.
The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr arises from coupling between temperature-dependent local lattice distortions and residual thermal stresses.
Thermal-expansion mismatch generates residual stresses in HfNbTaTiZr.
At high temperature, thermal expansion relaxes local lattice distortions.
Relaxation of local lattice distortions lowers creep resistance by reducing resistance to dislocation motion.
At lower temperatures and after cold working, enhanced local strain fields increase dislocation pinning.
Local lattice distortions and residual stresses lead to a higher elastic modulus.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C may induce short-range atomic ordering.
Short-range ordering produced during aging further pins dislocations and increases strength.
A stress-relieving anneal partially reduces the residual stresses present in the as-cast alloy.
After identical cold rolling, as-cast samples will have higher microhardness than stress-relieved samples.
As-cast samples will exhibit a steeper low-temperature elastic-modulus trend than stress-relieved samples.
As-cast samples will have lower tensile-creep rates at approximately 1250 °C than stress-relieved samples.
Aging at 600–800 °C will accentuate the predicted hardness, elastic-modulus, and creep differences through additional dislocation pinning.
The proposed mechanism operates from room temperature through approximately 1250 °C, including the 293–1100 K modulus range and the 600–800 °C aging range.
The proposed mechanism is especially relevant when composite solidification produces substantial thermal-expansion-mismatch stresses.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as homogenized, whereas the experimental control and baseline are described as as-cast. These are distinct processing states, so it is unclear which state defines the starting alloy.

The mechanism states that high-temperature relaxation of distortion lowers creep resistance, but the prediction assigns lower creep rates at 1250 °C to the more highly stressed as-cast state. The hypothesis does not explain why the proposed high-temperature relaxation would preserve this residual-stress-dependent creep difference.
